title: When Will Lawyers Trust AI? — Gabe Pereyra (Harvey)
pub: AAA — AI and the Future of Law (YouTube)
author: Gabe Pereyra

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Pereyra does not accept the cluster’s central framing that automation is likely to erode expertise reproduction. He argues instead that removing low-level work can accelerate associate development, while constructively proposing institution-specific tutoring and simulated matters to replace or improve parts of traditional training. These are predictions and design proposals, not demonstrated training outcomes.
qs: And so I think what’s actually going to happen is you’re going to be able to train associates sooner, and you’re going to be able to push associates up into doing the things that humans can uniquely do.

You could say, “I want to run a simulated fund formation, a simulated litigation, a simulated merger,” and go through the process end to end, getting feedback from a simulated client and simulated partners.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Pereyra rejects the premise that automating low-level work necessarily weakens lawyer development, arguing that much of the removed work has little educational value. He redirects the pipeline concern toward AI-enabled simulation, feedback and earlier exposure to complex work, while presenting faster learning as a prediction rather than an established result.
qs: I think the part where I’m super optimistic is that typically the work getting written off is the lowest value in terms of educational value.

You could say, “I want to run a simulated fund formation, a simulated litigation, a simulated merger,” and go through the process end to end, getting feedback from a simulated client and simulated partners.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source does not address whether AI uptake can close the justice gap or translate productivity into meaningful legal access. It instead forecasts AI-enabled professional training, workflow adaptation and larger law firms, so its position on the cluster’s central access-to-justice proposition cannot be determined.
qs: To me, the question isn’t, “What are these associates going to do?” It’s: how do they work in this new way so they can use this technology to get more leverage?
But I think a lot of the challenge is going to be that you need to learn to work in this new way, more than this being a simple swap-in replacement for any type of labor.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: Pereyra’s frequent personal AI use and identified difficulty supplying context are consistent with iterative experimentation and implementation caution, but the excerpt does not address practitioner-led legal-work redesign, shared governance, reliability, access to justice or judicial legitimacy. It therefore provides too little evidence to establish a position on the cluster’s broader proposition.
qs: I mean, obviously I use ChatGPT and all these products a ton.
But I found kind of one thing that’s missing from them is it’s still quite hard to get context into them.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source characterises the moment as one of unprecedented change but offers no recommendation that lawyers should actively shape AI deployment, pursue sustained learning, support implementation or participate in governance. It therefore neither clearly accepts nor rejects the cluster’s engagement-first proposition.
qs: We’re living through unprecedented change, and we’re really grateful to you for sharing your perspective.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: The source accepts agentic AI as end-to-end, multistep work and materially extends the cluster by proposing simulated legal matters to train both agents and lawyers. It also reinforces the need to shift verification toward auditable, explainable processes, though its claimed learning benefits remain predictive rather than demonstrated.
qs: You could say, “I want to run a simulated fund formation, a simulated litigation, a simulated merger,” and go through the process end to end, getting feedback from a simulated client and simulated partners.
Gabe Pereyra: I strongly agree with the auditability and explainability point.

st.t: Billable hour: Faster matters need not reduce profits
st.an: Pereyra accepts the core proposition that AI-driven efficiency need not undermine hourly-billing profits and supplies a concrete mechanism: automate work clients already refuse to pay for, then redeploy associate capacity. He also extends the synthesis with observed hybrid billing and a practice-specific rather than universal pricing approach, while presenting profitability gains as a proposed mechanism rather than measured results.
qs: But when I think about how these law firms are going to get more profitable, I think there is actually a huge amount of optimization you can do within the billable hour framework.

The private equity firms will say, “That work—I’m not going to pay for it.”  And so if you can go and say, “Well, here’s an agent or here’s a system that will do all of that work,” you can reallocate that associate time.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Pereyra accepts the cluster’s core view that AI should reshape organisational delivery rather than merely automate individual tasks, while reinforcing auditability and differentiated pricing. He materially extends the apprenticeship analysis by proposing end-to-end simulated matters as shared training infrastructure, though his claims about faster learning and larger firms remain analogy-based predictions rather than demonstrated legal-sector outcomes.
qs: And a lot of the value of the product is going to be: how do you make these law firms more profitable, not just how do you make individual lawyers more productive?

You could say, “I want to run a simulated fund formation, a simulated litigation, a simulated merger,” and go through the process end to end, getting feedback from a simulated client and simulated partners.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Pereyra accepts that legal AI’s value lies in language-intensive workflows, enterprise-grade contextual infrastructure and lawyer supervision rather than autonomous delivery. He materially extends the cluster by arguing that firms can repurpose existing review structures and embed institutional expertise in firm-specific systems that improve work and train associates, although these claims remain largely observational or forward-looking.
qs: And downstream from that, the same way you check the work of junior partners and senior associates, there’s a lot of that structure you can leverage.

So what we want to help firms do is take all of that internal expertise and build systems that are unique to them—systems they can use not just to do legal work better, but to distill the firm’s expertise into their more junior associates.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Pereyra accepts the cluster’s task-reconfiguration and protected-learning framing, then materially extends it by proposing realistic, feedback-rich client-matter simulations as shared infrastructure for training both legal AI agents and lawyers. This offers a concrete response to apprenticeship risks, although his claims about accelerated learning remain predictive rather than empirically established.
qs: You could say, “I want to run a simulated fund formation, a simulated litigation, a simulated merger,” and go through the process end to end, getting feedback from a simulated client and simulated partners.
What’s interesting is that this infrastructure trains agents—but it also trains humans.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Pereyra accepts the cluster’s organisational-redesign framing and materially extends it: AI should support firm-wide coordination, scalable delivery, auditability and new learning systems rather than merely improve individual productivity or replace labour. His claims are forward-looking and experience-based, not measured transformation outcomes.
qs: And a lot of the value of the product is going to be: how do you make these law firms more profitable, not just how do you make individual lawyers more productive?
But I think a lot of the challenge is going to be that you need to learn to work in this new way, more than this being a simple swap-in replacement for any type of labor.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: Pereyra reinforces the application-layer thesis by identifying security, privacy, governance, ethical walls and regulatory compliance as legal-specific infrastructure required for institutional deployment. He also cautions against inferring labour substitution from Harvey’s valuation, though he does not directly establish or evaluate durable competitive defensibility.
qs: Gabe Pereyra: The way I would think of Harvey now is we are building a platform that lets large law firms—and now actually law firms of any size—or in-house legal teams deploy generative AI at scale.

A lot of the product and platform problems you need to solve are not just, “How do you build a good product for an individual lawyer?”  It’s all of the security, data, privacy, governance, ethical walls—all of the regulatory challenges—everything you need so that a large law firm can use this with confidence.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: Pereyra supports the cluster’s core framing of Harvey as organisation-wide legal-AI infrastructure that augments legal teams and delegates selected work to agents rather than autonomously delivering complete matters. His emphasis on enterprise deployment, governance, verification and human accountability aligns closely with the synthesis, while his faster-training and largely-solved supervised-trust claims are optimistic predictions rather than measured outcomes.
qs: Gabe Pereyra: The way I would think of Harvey now is we are building a platform that lets large law firms—and now actually law firms of any size—or in-house legal teams deploy generative AI at scale.
One—which is kind of how Harvey is used—is human-in-the-loop, the same way that a partner would work with a team of associates.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: Pereyra supports the synthesis’s core view that useful legal AI depends on lawyer-like workflows, explainability, trained human supervision and client-specific judgment rather than model output alone. He also treats end-to-end automation and simulated training as future possibilities, consistent with retaining human checkpoints and distinguishing proposals from demonstrated outcomes.
qs: Now when you get a mistake, it’s not just, “Oh, it generated a bunch of text and I don’t know what happened.”  You can say, “Here is the reasoning trace.”  You can see, “Oh, it pulled the wrong case,” or “It summarized the case incorrectly.” Now you understand why it came to the wrong conclusion.

They do have deep technical expertise and they supervise teams—but a lot of their value is understanding the client, understanding the business implications of decisions, and understanding trade-offs.

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: Pereyra directly supports the cluster’s account of Harvey evolving from an individual productivity tool into firm-wide legal AI infrastructure, with security, privacy, governance and ethical walls enabling trusted deployment. He also frames Harvey as augmentation rather than proven labour substitution, while his claims about training and capability gains remain predictive or anecdotal rather than measured evidence of accuracy or productivity.
qs: Gabe Pereyra: The way I would think of Harvey now is we are building a platform that lets large law firms—and now actually law firms of any size—or in-house legal teams deploy generative AI at scale.

A lot of the product and platform problems you need to solve are not just, “How do you build a good product for an individual lawyer?”  It’s all of the security, data, privacy, governance, ethical walls—all of the regulatory challenges—everything you need so that a large law firm can use this with confidence.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: Pereyra supports the core proposition that improved legal AI still makes logical errors, while Leonard’s verification-cost question aligns with the cluster’s disputed productivity problem. The source is conceptual rather than empirical and does not establish that verification can never be eliminated in future autonomous workflows.
qs: As the models get better, the reasoning improves, but they still make logical mistakes.

Now some of the conversations we’re having are about reasoning hallucinations and whether the juice is worth the squeeze if a partner has to read an entire case just to make sure the AI accurately summarized what the case stands for.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: Pereyra supports the cluster’s view that legal AI value depends on workflow fit and sustained, lawyer-guided implementation rather than model capability alone. He treats proficiency as a learned practice, cites intensive use by experienced partners, and offers qualitative observations rather than quantified evidence of broad transformation.
qs: You had tools that didn’t fit your workflow, and you had to force your work into them.
You can give people guides and best practices, but it’s like teaching someone to use an iPhone—you only really learn by using it every day.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that AI is accelerating broader changes in legal business models while making auditability and explainability prerequisites for trusted deployment. Its claims are mainly conceptual and anecdotal, not evidence of completed market-wide transformation.
qs: AI, to me, just accelerates that change and shift.
Gabe Pereyra: I strongly agree with the auditability and explainability point.

st.t: Personalized coaching: Perceived follow-through lacks validated outcomes
st.an: The source directly supports the proposition that accumulated personal context can make general-purpose AI feel useful as an individualized coach. Pereyra and McCormack report tailored workout, fitness and nutrition guidance, but their evidence remains anecdotal and does not validate clinical, workplace or professional outcomes.
qs: And so every day I’ll be like, “What workout should I do based on all these factors?” And so it’s like a running workout log and journal.

And it’s so helpful because once it has all this data about you and information about you—and we also upload all of our health documents because we want all of the benefit of all of the feedback—it’s really incredible.

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: Pereyra supports the cluster’s central proposition by distinguishing individual-lawyer productivity from organisation-wide deployment and arguing that scaled adoption depends on institutional infrastructure and safeguards. The source does not, however, address whether usage volume demonstrates value or provide measured evidence of outcomes.
qs: Gabe Pereyra: The way I would think of Harvey now is we are building a platform that lets large law firms—and now actually law firms of any size—or in-house legal teams deploy generative AI at scale.

A lot of the product and platform problems you need to solve are not just, “How do you build a good product for an individual lawyer?”  It’s all of the security, data, privacy, governance, ethical walls—all of the regulatory challenges—everything you need so that a large law firm can use this with confidence.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Pereyra supports the cluster’s core claim that AI value depends on organisational redesign rather than model access or simple labour substitution. He advocates organisation-wide deployment, auditable human-in-the-loop workflows, repeated practical use and redesigned training, while treating autonomous complex legal work, larger firms and accelerated learning as expectations rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: But I think a lot of the challenge is going to be that you need to learn to work in this new way, more than this being a simple swap-in replacement for any type of labor.
One—which is kind of how Harvey is used—is human-in-the-loop, the same way that a partner would work with a team of associates.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: Pereyra endorses lawyer-supervised augmentation: models can generate routine work while experts review outputs and contribute higher-order judgment beyond drafting. He also recognizes persistent reasoning errors and treats end-to-end automation as a longer-term prospect. His optimism about accelerated junior learning and relatively low review costs represents a favorable view within—not a rejection of—the cluster’s acknowledged tensions.
qs: As the models get better, the reasoning improves, but they still make logical mistakes.
The way I think about it—both for engineering and for lawyers—is that people overly associate the job with producing text.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Pereyra accepts the cluster’s core augmentation thesis: AI changes how legal work is produced and scaled rather than simply replacing lawyers. He also aligns with hybrid pricing, human supervision and organisational integration, while taking a more optimistic view of firm growth and associate development and a more defensive view of hourly billing.
qs: But I think a lot of the challenge is going to be that you need to learn to work in this new way, more than this being a simple swap-in replacement for any type of labor.

They do have deep technical expertise and they supervise teams—but a lot of their value is understanding the client, understanding the business implications of decisions, and understanding trade-offs.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Pereyra supports the proposition that AI can take over drafting and information-structuring tasks while senior lawyers retain review and higher-level problem-solving roles. His account reinforces complementarity and the economics of verification, but does not establish whether this will preserve junior staffing or overall employment.
qs: The reason law firms and engineering teams are structured the way they are—where junior people do the drafting and senior people review—is because it’s exponentially less effort to review work than to generate it from scratch.
We’re bottlenecked by very senior people who can create abstractions, come up with product ideas, scale complex systems, and understand very complex business problems.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Pereyra strongly supports selective, human-supervised deployment: he treats augmentation and verification as the present model, distinguishes bounded routine tasks from complex matters, and expects work and business models to be redesigned rather than lawyers or hourly billing uniformly displaced. His claims are principally experiential and predictive rather than controlled evidence, but align with the cluster’s core proposition.
qs: One—which is kind of how Harvey is used—is human-in-the-loop, the same way that a partner would work with a team of associates.

I think for very complex work—that’s what most of the law firms we work with focus on—I don’t see a world, even in the next decade, where for an antitrust litigation or a very complex acquisition you’re able to trust these systems end to end.

st.t: Workflow trust: Verification remains costly and contested
st.an: Pereyra supports the cluster’s core view that trust is created through supervised workflows and governance rather than error-free AI. He treats verification as sufficient for current augmentation while acknowledging that unfamiliar reasoning errors can make review costly, and he limits autonomous reliance to bounded tasks with demonstrated performance.
qs: One—which is kind of how Harvey is used—is human-in-the-loop, the same way that a partner would work with a team of associates.

Now some of the conversations we’re having are about reasoning hallucinations and whether the juice is worth the squeeze if a partner has to read an entire case just to make sure the AI accurately summarized what the case stands for.

kp.k: Harvey shifts from individual productivity to enterprise coordination
kp.d: Pereyra describes Harvey as a platform for law firms of any size and in-house legal teams, with enterprise deployment requiring security, privacy, governance, ethical walls and regulatory safeguards. He presents collaboration across deal teams and clients, firm profitability and better legal outcomes at scale as the emerging value proposition, rather than individual productivity alone.
qs: The way I would think of Harvey now is we are building a platform that lets large law firms—and now actually law firms of any size—or in-house legal teams deploy generative AI at scale.
It’s all of the security, data, privacy, governance, ethical walls—all of the regulatory challenges—everything you need so that a large law firm can use this with confidence.
And a lot of the value of the product is going to be: how do you make these law firms more profitable, not just how do you make individual lawyers more productive?

kp.k: Billable hours persist alongside practice-specific hybrid pricing
kp.d: Pereyra rejects a straightforward prediction that AI will end hourly billing: it standardizes pricing for services whose client value is difficult to determine, and clients sometimes prefer it to fixed fees. He reports emerging hybrid arrangements, such as fixed-fee merger diligence with other work billed hourly, and expects solutions to vary by practice, firm size, geography, industry and client rather than converge on one replacement model.
qs: I’m actually somewhat skeptical that this is the death of the billable hour.
The biggest problem the billable hour solves is: here is a super standardized way to price services that are very difficult to price.
What we are starting to see is just hybrid billing.
We’ll do the diligence fixed fee,

kp.k: Automation can improve profitability without abandoning hourly billing
kp.d: Drawing on conversations with private equity firms and their law firms, Pereyra reports that first-year associate work on fund formation is sometimes written off regardless of the work performed. He argues that automating such work and reallocating associates, reducing cap overruns and addressing disputed research charges can improve profitability within existing billing structures. These are customer observations and proposed mechanisms, not quantified profitability findings.
qs: in a lot of cases all the first-year associate work gets written off just right off the bat. It doesn’t even matter what work they do.
you can reallocate that associate time. That is actually making you more profitable.
Some of these projects are capped. And so if you go over the cap, you’re losing money.
The realization rates aren’t 100% because you argue with the clients and they’ll say, “I’m not going to pay for that amount of legal research.”

kp.k: Delegation may accelerate rather than undermine associate development
kp.d: Pereyra argues that written-off tasks usually have low educational value and predicts that delegating them to AI will move associates sooner into higher-level work. His supporting analogy is Harvey’s engineering team, where he reports faster learning and more complex assignments as models handle lower-level coding. He identifies team orchestration and knowing when to review as skills shared by senior engineers and legal partners; the legal training outcome remains a prediction.
qs: I think the part where I’m super optimistic is that typically the work getting written off is the lowest value in terms of educational value.

They’re actually learning faster. They’re able to work at a higher level of abstraction and take on more complex projects because they’re able to delegate a lot of this lower-level work to the models.

And so I think what’s actually going to happen is you’re going to be able to train associates sooner, and you’re going to be able to push associates up into doing the things that humans can uniquely do.

kp.k: Augmentation could enable larger firms, not simple labor replacement
kp.d: Leonard frames Harvey’s stated $8 billion valuation as implying labor substitution and asks about hiring associates three or four years ahead. Pereyra explicitly disputes that interpretation. Using Salesforce as an analogy, he predicts that better coordination will allow much larger law firms and emphasizes learning new workflows rather than swapping software for labor. He does not specify future associate-to-partner ratios or hiring reductions.
qs: You know, Harvey is valued now at an $8 billion valuation. So it’s being priced more as a labor substitute than just a mere software tool.
One point I would make is it’s not clear to me that our valuation implies labor substitution.

I expect what you’ll see is that there will actually be much larger law firms, because I think this technology will let you scale law firms much more the same way Salesforce did with sales organizations.
you need to learn to work in this new way, more than this being a simple swap-in replacement for any type of labor.

kp.k: Human verification distinguishes augmentation from autonomous legal reliance
kp.d: Pereyra describes Harvey as human-in-the-loop: output is tracked and checked, analogous to a partner reviewing associate work. He reports that hallucinations have not really blocked use during the past year and asserts that the industry has largely solved trust for this supervised mode. He explicitly distinguishes that assertion from trusting legal output directly, which he regards as harder and outside Harvey’s current focus; he does not claim that errors have been eliminated.
qs: The partner is never directly sending associate work to the client without checking, and I would still think very much that that is how Harvey is used.
And I would say in that sense, actually, in the past year, we haven’t really had hallucinations be a blocker for using this technology.
And so I would say we’ve actually—not we as in Harvey, but we as an industry—largely solved that trust problem.
how do we directly trust the legal output of these systems. And that, I think, we’re not there.

kp.k: Autonomous trust depends on track records and task complexity
kp.d: By analogy with self-driving cars, Pereyra argues that demonstrated performance on defined tasks could eventually justify direct reliance on AI. He predicts that in the next couple of years systems may generate binding NDAs using both parties’ historical data and precedent without checking, but does not foresee end-to-end reliance for antitrust litigation or complex acquisitions even in the next decade. These are differentiated forecasts, not demonstrated capabilities.
qs: At the end of the day, the way you trust a self-driving car is just its track record.

You can look at statistical results of their performance, and at some point you can build confidence and say, “For this set of tasks, this performs on par with a human, and I’m comfortable with this making a binding decision.”

But I think there will be low-level work—like, for example, NDAs—where the systems in the next couple of years will get to the point where you’ll probably just be able to say, “I want to enter into an NDA with this company.”
I don’t see a world, even in the next decade, where for an antitrust litigation or a very complex acquisition you’re able to trust these systems end to end.

kp.k: AAA arbitration illustrates bounded, supervised multi-agent deployment
kp.d: McCormack reports that AAA has built what she calls the first AI arbitrator, comprising twenty or thirty—or forty, depending on case complexity—agents across an arbitration process. She describes an initial specific use case and expresses confidence particularly for contained documents-only disputes aligned with training data. She subsequently clarifies that it has a human in the loop and identifies auditable records and governance as foundations of trust; no performance study is supplied.
qs: Just by way of background, at the AAA we have built the first AI arbitrator. It’s really twenty or thirty—or forty, depending on how complicated the case—different agents that operate across an arbitration process.
It can—especially a documents-only dispute that’s pretty contained to the type of data it’s been trained on.
I should be clear—our generative AI arbitrator does have a human in the loop, because I think that is important.
If the agents you’ve built are auditable and you have a trail that you can show—a record you can show—I think that is how we get there.

kp.k: Legal supervision practices inform explainable AI governance
kp.d: Pereyra recommends adapting law firms’ existing systems for coordinating specialists, showing work, citing sources and reviewing work product. He argues that legal output must remain intelligible to courts and counterparties, providing a constraint even as models improve. His comparison with human expertise and the stock market supports an argument for governability, not a finding that existing AI explanations guarantee correctness.
qs: They’ve built these incredible systems of: this is how you do citations, this is how you show your work, this is how you decompose the work product.
What we’ve seen law firms do really well is take all of the expertise and systems they’ve built to coordinate teams of lawyers and start thinking about what parts of that they can repurpose.
At the end of the day, the language you produce in legal needs to be understandable by the counterparty or the court.
But for legal, we’re still a ways off from that.

kp.k: Regulatory barriers redirected Harvey away from consumer legal access
kp.d: Pereyra says Harvey initially explored consumer law to expand legal access, but its investigation of US regulatory issues led it to conclude that it could not offer model-delivered legal advice, illustrated by eviction assistance. He contrasts this with ad hoc consumer use of ChatGPT, notes changes in Arizona and Utah, and leaves consumer services as a future ambition while prioritizing firms and enterprises. These are his account and regulatory characterizations, not cited legal holdings.
qs: When we started the company, we actually started looking at consumer law, and we wanted to use generative AI to massively expand legal access.
Then we did this deep dive into all of the regulatory issues in the U.S., and the conclusion was: you can’t use these models to give legal advice.
And now with ChatGPT, this is kind of happening ad hoc.
There’s Arizona, Utah—I think there are some states where they’re starting to allow some forms of this.
But right now we’re still much more focused on law firms and enterprises.

kp.k: AI accelerates existing investment and legal-business changes
kp.d: McCormack describes growing private equity interest and state openness to new legal-business models. Pereyra agrees that AI accelerates pre-existing trends, reports working with private equity firms and a recent conversation with a private-equity-backed personal injury firm seeking aggressive expansion, and notes companies building AI-first law firms. He expects regulatory and business-model variation across countries and consumer versus enterprise markets, rather than a single trajectory.
qs: Our general sense is that most of these trends were already happening before generative AI got very popular, and then, in different aspects, AI accelerates them greatly.
I talked with a personal injury firm just yesterday that has a private equity backer, and they’re looking to scale really aggressively.
There are companies trying to build AI-first law firms.
There are so many different angles—consumer legal services will look different, enterprise services will look different.

kp.k: Practitioners must learn models’ unfamiliar reasoning error patterns
kp.d: Pereyra distinguishes missing-information errors from continuing logical mistakes, stressing that model reasoning failures differ from human ones. He reports that approximately twenty lawyers hired after his brother joined the product team have developed highly accurate expectations of these errors. He presents training and repeated use as central remedies; this is an internal observational claim, not a measured hallucination rate or proof that all reasoning errors are predictable.
qs: As the models get better, the reasoning improves, but they still make logical mistakes.
They don’t make the same logical errors that humans do.
We’ve since hired about twenty other lawyers to help build the product.
If you talk to them, their mental model of the reasoning errors these systems make is almost perfect.
You can develop that same mental model—but it takes training.

kp.k: Lawyer-like research agents aim to make errors traceable
kp.d: Pereyra describes building systems that follow legal research steps: finding seminal cases, reading and summarizing them, locating supporting cases and relevant client analogues, and linking credible sources. He argues that this improves problem-solving and explainability by allowing reviewers to identify a wrong case or incorrect summary in a reasoning trace. The transcript gives a design rationale rather than comparative accuracy measurements.
qs: They would find the seminal cases. They would read those cases and summarize them.
They would use Westlaw or Lexis to do that search.
That’s what these reasoning models or agents are doing. So a lot of what we’re building is: how do we build systems that reason like a lawyer?
You can see, “Oh, it pulled the wrong case,” or “It summarized the case incorrectly.” Now you understand why it came to the wrong conclusion.

kp.k: Imperfect drafts can remain useful under expert review
kp.d: Pereyra argues that useful AI need not be perfectly correct because generating a draft costs more effort than reviewing it. His personal writing example is a 60–80% draft, not a legal accuracy statistic. He reports partners assigning the same task to an associate and a model and reviewing both, sometimes recognizing a correct structured answer immediately and sometimes identifying work requiring further delegation.
qs: Even though it’s not perfect, it’s like a 60–80% draft. It gives you structure, which is incredibly valuable.

The reason law firms and engineering teams are structured the way they are—where junior people do the drafting and senior people review—is because it’s exponentially less effort to review work than to generate it from scratch.
What we’re seeing partners do now is give a task to an associate and give the same task to the model.
They can review both quickly.

kp.k: Senior legal value shifts beyond document production
kp.d: In response to McCormack’s hypothetical about models outperforming lawyers, Pereyra argues that partners’ value includes technical expertise, supervision, client understanding, business implications and trade-offs rather than drafting alone. He predicts continuing human work in designing governance and better legal systems, analogizing law to programming and mathematics as domains without a fixed ceiling, unlike his characterization of driving as a bounded task.
qs: On the legal side, the value of a partner is not that they can write the best briefs.

They do have deep technical expertise and they supervise teams—but a lot of their value is understanding the client, understanding the business implications of decisions, and understanding trade-offs.
you can automate things like NDAs or arbitration, but you still need to design the systems that govern those processes.
I think this technology will keep pushing people to higher levels of abstraction.

kp.k: Firm knowledge and simulations could transform legal training
kp.d: Pereyra reports current use of AI as personalized tutors, but argues that legal teaching is constrained by expertise residing inside firms rather than publicly, unlike much coding knowledge. He proposes incorporating feedback, practice guides and institutional knowledge, followed by simulated client matters with simulated partner and client feedback. He suggests reinforcement-learning environments could train both agents and humans, predicting faster learning by reducing low-value repetition; these simulations are presented as an opportunity, not an established outcome.
qs: It works less well for legal because most legal expertise lives inside law firms.
The first step is putting all the feedback, all the practice guides, all of that institutional knowledge into these systems so they can be used to train associates.

You could say, “I want to run a simulated fund formation, a simulated litigation, a simulated merger,” and go through the process end to end, getting feedback from a simulated client and simulated partners.
What’s interesting is that this infrastructure trains agents—but it also trains humans.
But over ten years, there’s a lot of repetition that isn’t high-value learning.

kp.k: Language interfaces and sustained practice drive adoption
kp.d: Asked about unexpectedly rapid lawyer adoption, Pereyra attributes it to generative AI fitting language-based work instead of forcing work into mismatched tools. He cites experienced senior partners, including Harvey adviser Gordon Moody, as effective early users and argues that deep legal expertise combined with extensive model use produces substantial capability differences. His recommendation is constant practical use to develop an error-aware mental model, rather than relying on guides alone; the evidence is anecdotal rather than an adoption survey.
qs: The simple answer is that this is the first time the technology has been centered around language.
Before this, legal technology wasn’t language-based. You had tools that didn’t fit your workflow, and you had to force your work into them.
What distinguishes those partners is how much they use the technology.
The skill gap between a first-time user and someone who has used these tools for hours a day over multiple years is enormous.
The only way to build that mental model is to use the technology constantly.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Pereyra presents AI chiefly as augmentation that changes firm economics, coordination, training and professional work, while predicting selective rather than universal autonomous legal services.
pts.d:
1. Enterprise deployment: Pereyra says Harvey has evolved from individual lawyer productivity toward an organisational platform supporting secure deployment, collaboration across teams and clients, firm profitability, and better, faster, more robust in-house legal outcomes at scale. He describes security, privacy, governance and ethical walls as central deployment problems.
2. Pricing and profitability: He doubts AI will eliminate hourly billing because it standardises the pricing of heterogeneous, hard-to-value services. He reports emerging hybrid arrangements, such as fixed-fee diligence alongside hourly transaction work. He argues AI can improve profitability within hourly billing by automating work clients will not pay for, reallocating associates, reducing cap overruns and limiting write-offs. He expects different combinations of software, hourly billing and fixed fees across practices and markets rather than one replacement model.
3. Firm scale and employment: He rejects the host's inference that Harvey's valuation establishes labour substitution. Using Salesforce as an analogy, he predicts AI-enabled coordination will permit much larger law firms. He frames the challenge as learning a new way of working rather than simply replacing a category of workers; he does not provide a numerical hiring or employment forecast.
4. Associate development: He argues that work written off by clients generally has low educational value, and predicts delegation of lower-level work to AI will accelerate associates' development toward orchestration, review and more complex work. He reports current use of AI as a tutor and proposes firm-specific systems incorporating internal feedback, practice guides and institutional knowledge. His further prediction is that simulated matters with simulated client and partner feedback will train both agents and humans and dramatically accelerate learning.
5. Supervised trust versus direct reliance: He says hallucinations have largely ceased to block adoption in human-in-the-loop settings, where AI work remains tracked and checked through firm processes. This is not a claim that hallucinations have disappeared. He distinguishes that position from trusting legal outputs directly, which he considers substantially harder. He predicts routine NDAs could become binding without human checking, but does not expect end-to-end reliance for antitrust litigation or very complex acquisitions within the next decade.
6. Verification and reasoning: He argues that lawyers can repurpose existing supervisory structures, citations, decomposed work and explanations to check AI. He acknowledges non-intuitive logical errors distinct from fabricated facts or citations. He says practical experience develops a mental model of these errors, while agents that research through lawyer-like steps and provide source-linked traces make mistakes easier to diagnose. He further claims imperfect drafts can still be useful because reviewing work takes much less effort than generating it.
7. Continuing professional value: He argues senior lawyers' enduring value lies in understanding clients, business implications and trade-offs, coordinating expertise, and designing governance systems rather than producing documents alone. He predicts AI will push lawyers toward higher levels of abstraction and better legal-system design rather than exhaust the domain's opportunities.
8. Market structure and consumer access: He characterises AI as accelerating pre-existing regulatory and business-model changes, including interest in private-equity-backed firms and AI-first law firms. He recounts that regulatory concerns deterred Harvey's initial consumer-law ambitions, while consumers now obtain legal guidance through ChatGPT ad hoc. He expresses a future ambition to support consumers but says Harvey currently concentrates on law firms and enterprises. He expects consumer and enterprise services, and developments across jurisdictions, to differ.
9. Adoption and proficiency: He attributes relatively rapid adoption in law to the fit between language-based AI and legal workflows. He reports substantial use by senior partners, not merely juniors, and argues that sustained hands-on use creates a large proficiency gap between experienced and first-time users.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is predominantly Pereyra's company experience, customer conversations, illustrative workflows and cross-domain analogies; no formal legal-performance or labour-market study is presented.
pts.d: For pricing and profitability, Pereyra cites conversations with partners, large private equity firms and their law firms, including fund-formation work where first-year time is written off, capped projects and clients disputing research charges. These are qualitative examples rather than quantified savings or realisation results. For larger firms, he uses Salesforce's coordination role as an analogy, not evidence of measured AI-driven law-firm expansion. For faster associate development, he draws principally on Harvey engineers reportedly learning faster through delegation; the transfer to legal training is a prediction. He also reports lawyers using Harvey to ask how to structure fund documents, and discussions with people at Stanford and elsewhere about simulation-based training; he reports no completed training trial or measured acceleration. For trust and reasoning, he invokes Harvey's deployment experience, existing partner-associate review practices, and product-team lawyers' acquired familiarity with model errors. His statement that their mental models are nearly perfect is an informal assessment, not a benchmark. He describes agents' research steps and traces, and reports partners comparing associate and model outputs, without providing measured accuracy or verification costs. His '60–80% draft' description concerns his own writing experience, not a legal benchmark. For eventual direct reliance, self-driving cars' statistical track records are a proposed analogy for establishing confidence, not evidence that autonomous legal services have achieved comparable reliability. For market change, he cites Harvey's early regulatory investigation, conversations with private equity firms and a recent conversation with a private-equity-backed personal injury firm. The legal restrictions he recounts are his characterisation, not independently substantiated legal conclusions in the interview. For adoption, he offers the named example of Gordon Moody using models extensively and wider observations of transactional and litigation firms. Predictions about unchecked NDAs, the decade-long boundary for complex work and enduring senior-lawyer value are reasoned expectations rather than findings from supplied data.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Pereyra distinguishes current supervised use from prospective routine autonomy in the next couple of years, while rejecting complex end-to-end reliance even within the next decade.
pts.d: All relative periods refer to the interview labelled 2026 in the supplied document. Current or emerging developments include hybrid pricing, profitability work with firms, lawyer tutoring, product-team expertise in model errors and senior-partner adoption. He places Harvey's initial individual-productivity focus around three to three and a half years before the interview. His assertion that hallucinations have not been an adoption blocker concerns the preceding year and specifically supervised use; it assumes tracked outputs and organisational checks that stop errors reaching clients. It does not extend to direct reliance or establish an absence of fabricated material. For lower-level work such as NDAs, he predicts potentially unchecked execution 'in the next couple of years,' conditional on access to both parties' historical data, precedent and sufficient performance. For complex antitrust litigation and acquisitions, he explicitly does not foresee end-to-end trust even in the next decade. More generally, autonomous reliance would require a task-specific performance track record sufficient to support confidence in binding decisions. The billing transition, larger firms and accelerated training have no fixed completion dates. Pricing depends on practice area, firm size, industry, country, region and clients. Faster development depends on delegating low-value work, learning orchestration, and building usable training systems; firm-specific tutoring is constrained by legal expertise residing inside firms rather than publicly available sources. Simulation-based training is presented as a next opportunity, not established routine practice. Effective verification depends on lawyer familiarity with models, explainability and auditable work processes. Consumer expansion remains a future ambition conditioned by regulation, with Arizona and Utah mentioned as settings of change. The claimed proficiency advantage depends on extensive repeated use over time.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law firms, associates, partners, in-house teams and enterprise clients; consumer access is a separate, regulation-dependent opportunity.
pts.d: Law firms of any size are within Harvey's stated platform scope, although much of Pereyra's discussion concerns large firms, numerous concurrent matters, and complex transactional or litigation work. Firm leaders would redesign collaboration, supervision and practice-specific economics, potentially increasing profitability and organisational scale; his account does not quantify changes in associate-to-partner staffing ratios. Associates would delegate low-level work, acquire coordination and review skills earlier, and potentially train through firm-specific tutors and simulated matters. Partners and senior associates would remain responsible for checking outputs and would place greater emphasis on client judgment, business trade-offs, team coordination and system governance. Both junior and senior lawyers would need repeated practical use to develop proficiency and recognise model-specific errors. In-house legal teams, including Fortune 500 departments, are buyers seeking secure deployment and better outcomes at scale, not law-firm providers. Enterprise clients, including private equity funds, affect the economics through refusal to pay for junior work, fee caps and billing disputes; routine NDA counterparties are the example of possible future direct automated contracting. Private-equity-backed and AI-first law firms represent potential new or expanding delivery models, distinct from Harvey's role as a software platform. Individuals with unmet legal needs, illustrated by people facing eviction, are a separate prospective beneficiary group: Pereyra describes consumer legal access as an original ambition constrained by regulation, not an existing Harvey consumer service. His engineering examples concern Harvey's engineers and serve as analogies for legal training and professional value.
